title: Rack-wide content-hash page fabric: one physical copy per rack
idea: Inverts 'memory is private to each host': a CXL 3.x switch keeps a hash-indexed page directory so identical 4 KB pages (OS images, shared libraries, model weights, zero pages) across every server in a rack map to one physical copy in a pooled tier, with copy-on-write on store. Hashing runs in the switch ASIC at line rate, so no host CPU scans pages as per-host KSM does.
why: Capacity: cloud VM fleets show 20-40% cross-VM duplicate pages, and inference fleets holding identical weights collapse N replicas to ~1 per rack, so DRAM per rack drops 1.3-3x.

title: One latent per token regenerates every layer's K/V on demand
idea: Inverts 'each layer stores its own KV cache': DRAM holds a single low-rank latent per token (e.g., 256 dims), and each layer's tensor cores up-project it to K and V just in time inside the attention kernel, spending cheap FLOPs to save scarce bytes. A short distillation pass retrofits existing models so the shared cross-layer latent is trained jointly.
why: KV-cache bytes drop 10-40x vs per-layer FP16 KV, beyond per-layer latent attention, so long-context serving fits in a fraction of the HBM/DRAM.

title: OS lossy heap: applications declare error tolerance per allocation
idea: Inverts 'memory must be bit-exact': a new mmap flag (MAP_LOSSY plus an error bound) sends ML activations, image buffers and analytics sketches to a region where the memory controller applies error-bounded floating-point compression (ZFP/SZ-style) on writeback. Exactness stays the default; lossy bytes are opt-in and typed.
why: 3-8x effective capacity on tolerant data, which is often 30-60% of an ML or media server's footprint.

title: Lineage paging: drop recomputable pages, rebuild them on fault
idea: Inverts 'data must be stored to be kept': the kernel records a lineage (source file + offset + transform such as decompress, JIT, parse or decode) for derived pages. Under pressure it evicts them without writing them anywhere, and on a fault it rebuilds them by replaying the transform on a spare core, like Spark lineage applied to the page cache and runtime heaps.
why: Derived data (decompressed caches, JIT code, parsed configs, decoded media) is often 15-30% of resident memory; reclaiming it with no swap I/O cuts DRAM need by that share.

title: Fiber-loop delay-line memory holds cold pages in flight
idea: Inverts 'memory is a place in space' into 'memory is time in flight': cold pages circulate in a DWDM fiber spool (10 km, 100 channels x 400 Gb/s, about 250 MB in flight per loop) with optical-electrical regeneration each lap, and a rack controller grabs a page as it passes. Average access is ~25 us, which suits far-memory tiers that today pin DRAM for cold pages.
why: Moves cold-tier bytes off DRAM onto glass and lasers, which are not supply-constrained; a wear-free swap tier that needs no DRAM wafers.

title: Canonicalized document KV shared across all tenants
idea: Inverts 'each request owns its KV cache': RAG chunks, tool schemas and system prompts are normalized into canonical position-independent KV blocks (re-rotated to the needed position at use) and stored once per cluster under a content hash, so any tenant that retrieves the same document reuses the same KV blocks.
why: In RAG and agent workloads 60-90% of context is shared documents, so KV memory per active user drops 5-20x.

title: Precision that ages: KV entries fade from FP16 to 2-bit
idea: Inverts 'a value keeps its precision for life': a background kernel demotes KV entries as they age or lose attention mass (FP16 to FP8 to INT4 to INT2), like a JPEG whose quality fades with distance, while recent and high-attention tokens stay sharp.
why: Average KV storage near 3 bits per element instead of 16: a 4-5x KV footprint cut at long context with small accuracy loss.

title: Hot-line compaction packs hot 64-byte lines from many pages
idea: Inverts 'the 4 KB page is the unit of placement': the memory controller tracks hotness per 64 B line and migrates hot lines from many sparse pages into dense DRAM 'hot pages' through a line-remap table, leaving the cold remainder of each page in CXL or flash tiers.
why: Typical pages have only 10-25% hot lines, so page-granular tiering wastes the rest; line-granular placement cuts the DRAM needed for the same hit rate 2-3x.

title: Garbage collector living inside the memory expander
idea: Inverts 'GC is a host-CPU job that needs 2-3x heap headroom': a CXL Type-3 expander runs a concurrent copying/compacting collector next to its DRAM, with hardware forwarding pointers serving as the read barrier. Because it compacts continuously, managed heaps run at 1.1-1.3x live data.
why: Java/Go/.NET fleets reserve large heap headroom; shrinking it frees 30-50% of the DRAM those services occupy.

title: Internal GB-second market where memory-hungry jobs must bid
idea: Inverts 'memory is free once the server is bought': the cluster scheduler prices resident memory per GB-second at a spot price set by scarcity. Elastic consumers (caches, JVM heaps, prefetch buffers) register demand curves and shrink automatically when the price rises.
why: Fleets strand 25-40% of DRAM in over-requested allocations; price signals reclaim much of it with no new hardware.

title: Follow-the-moon: shift memory-heavy batch to regions with idle DRAM
idea: Inverts 'memory demand is local in time': a global scheduler moves memory-bound batch work (index builds, embedding generation, training-data prep) to datacenters in their night trough, where DRAM sits idle after interactive demand falls.
why: Interactive fleets are sized for diurnal peaks and leave 30-50% of DRAM idle off-peak; time-shifting avoids buying new DRAM for batch growth.

title: Entropy-coded weights decoded inside registers, never materialized
idea: Inverts 'data must be decompressed before compute': weights stay Huffman/ANS-coded in DRAM and HBM and are decoded per tile into shared memory or registers inside the matmul kernel. The main target is BF16/FP8 exponent fields, which carry only ~2-3 bits of entropy.
why: Lossless 1.3-1.6x cut in weight footprint with bit-identical outputs, and it stacks with quantization.

title: Local-loss training lets each block free activations immediately
idea: Inverts 'backprop must store every activation': blocks train on local objectives (per-block predictive or contrastive heads, plus a periodic short global sync), so each block's activations are freed as soon as its local update finishes.
why: Activation memory, often 50-80% of the training footprint at long sequence lengths, shrinks to about one block's worth: a 10-30x cut in activation memory.

title: Matryoshka weights that shrink themselves under memory pressure
idea: Inverts 'a deployed model has a fixed size': nested-width training lets a serving node evict the trailing slices of every weight matrix when DRAM is tight and reload them when it is not, trading a few points of quality for 2-4x less weight memory in real time.
why: An elastic footprint lets fleets size DRAM for average demand instead of peak.

title: Hibernate idle functions to flash between requests in under 1 ms
idea: Inverts 'a warm service must stay resident': after ~50 ms idle, an idle container's dirty pages are compressed and snapshotted to a CXL-attached flash tier, and the next request restores them lazily through userfaultfd prefetch of the recorded working set.
why: Serverless and microservice instances are idle >90% of the time; DRAM per hosted function drops 5-10x.

title: Erasure-coded in-memory stores instead of full replicas
idea: Inverts 'durability in memory means 2-3 full replicas': in-memory databases and caches store data as k+m erasure-coded stripes across nodes (e.g., 4+2) and rebuild them over RDMA when a node fails.
why: Replica DRAM overhead falls from 100-200% to ~50%, about a 2x fleet DRAM saving for replicated stores.

title: Landmark keys in DRAM, full KV blocks indexed on flash
idea: Inverts 'attention needs every past token resident': DRAM keeps one landmark key per 64-token block, and the full KV blocks sit on NVMe/CXL flash. Each decode step fetches only the top-k blocks whose landmarks score highest against the query.
why: Million-token contexts need DRAM for only ~2-5% of their KV: a 20-50x cut in KV DRAM.

title: Hardware base-relative 32-bit pointers in every load unit
idea: Inverts 'pointers are 64-bit absolute addresses': an ISA extension lets loads and stores take a 32-bit offset plus a per-region base register, so graphs, trees and object heaps store half-width pointers natively with no software decode cost.
why: Pointer-dense heaps shrink 25-45% (as JVM compressed oops show in software), across every language.

title: Optimizer states superposed inside count-sketch arrays
idea: Inverts 'each memory cell stores exactly one value': Adam moments for huge embedding and expert tables live in a few count-sketch arrays where many parameters share cells through signed hashes, and the median of the hashed reads recovers each parameter's moment.
why: Optimizer state, normally 2-3x the weight size, shrinks 5-20x for sparse or embedding-heavy models.

title: Weights stored as PRNG seeds plus a few coefficients
idea: Inverts 'weights are stored numbers': each block of weights is approximated as a combination of a few pseudo-random basis vectors that an on-chip LFSR generates from a stored seed, so DRAM holds seeds and 4-bit coefficients instead of weights.
why: Effective 2-3 bits per weight, trading cheap compute for memory; the generator costs a few gates per lane.

title: Value-range narrowing: JIT shrinks fields to the bits actually used
idea: Inverts 'a field's width is fixed by its declared type': a profiling JIT sees that int64/double fields hold small ranges (counters, enums, timestamps near now) and re-lays objects into bit-packed struct-of-arrays, with guard deoptimization if a value ever overflows.
why: Java, JS and Python heaps carry 40-70% unused high-order and padding bits; heaps shrink 1.5-2.5x with no programmer change.

title: Push queries into computational SSDs so buffer pools shrink
idea: Inverts 'a database must cache pages in DRAM to be fast': filters, projections and aggregations run inside SSD controllers next to the flash, so only qualifying rows reach host memory and the buffer pool is sized for results instead of the working set.
why: Analytical databases give 50-80% of server DRAM to buffer pools; pushdown can shrink that 3-10x for scan-heavy work.

title: Whole-block dataflow fusion keeps intermediates only in SRAM
idea: Inverts 'every operator writes its output to memory': a compiler fuses an entire transformer block (norm, QKV, attention, MLP) into one persistent streaming kernel that passes tiles core-to-core through on-chip SRAM, so intermediate activations never touch DRAM/HBM during inference.
why: Removes activation buffers and workspace (often 10-30% of inference memory) and the traffic they generate.

title: DIMM reincarnation: retired DDR4 behind 28 nm CXL bridges
idea: Inverts 'retired DIMMs are e-waste': hyperscalers pull DDR4 from decommissioned servers, retest it and mount it on CXL Type-3 cards whose controller is made on existing 28 nm logic lines. The result is a slow but large tier for cold pages and KV spill.
why: Millions of DDR4 DIMMs retire each year; reusing them adds 10-25% fleet capacity at near-zero cost per bit with no new DRAM wafers.

title: AI-grade binning: sell failing DRAM dies to fault-tolerant workloads
idea: Inverts 'every die must pass full spec': dies from existing lines that fail retention screens or have clustered bad rows get a per-die bad-row map in a 40 nm controller's fuse table. They are sold as 'AI-grade' modules for weights and KV, where row remapping plus tensor-level checksums hide the defects.
why: Recovers several % of wafer output that is now scrapped or downbinned, so existing fabs yield more usable bits with no new capacity.

title: 28 nm CXL controller with inline zero-line and base-delta compression
idea: Inverts 'compression costs host CPU cycles': a CXL expander ASIC built on existing 28 nm lines removes zero lines and applies base-delta-immediate compression per 64 B line, with a small metadata cache, and exposes about 2x the physical DRAM as logical capacity.
why: Hardware line compression yields 1.5-2.2x on server heaps and needs only trailing-node logic, not leading-edge DRAM.

title: Read-mostly tier on legacy SLC NAND for weights and code
idea: Inverts 'working memory needs unlimited endurance': weights, shared libraries and embedding tables are rarely written, so they are mapped byte-addressably onto pSLC NAND from depreciated 2D and early-3D NAND lines. A DRAM read cache sits in front, and a write-rate limiter enforces the endurance budget.
why: Read-mostly bytes are 30-60% of inference memory; moving them to existing NAND frees DRAM at ~1/10 the cost per bit.

title: Wide-slow capacity DRAM bins from trailing DRAM lines
idea: Inverts 'DRAM must hit speed bins': existing 2x/1x-nm DDR4 lines run to relaxed timing specs (longer tRCD, lower clock) and allow more repaired rows, tuned for CXL capacity tiers whose latency is already ~200 ns. Looser bins raise yield and the share of each wafer that can be sold.
why: Raises usable bit output of existing trailing DRAM fabs 10-20% and supplies far-memory tiers without leading-edge wafers.

title: Gist tokens compress idle conversation context into learned summaries
idea: Inverts 'context must be kept as raw per-token KV': when a session goes idle, a small trained compressor squeezes its KV into a few dozen 'gist' states that condition the model almost equivalently when the user returns. It is software only and runs on GPUs already installed.
why: Resident KV for idle multi-turn sessions drops 10-50x, so existing hardware can hold far more concurrent users.

title: Zygote fork: preinitialize runtimes once, copy-on-write everywhere
idea: Inverts 'each container boots its own runtime': as with Android's zygote, each node keeps a pre-warmed Python/JVM/ML-framework process with libraries and shared weights loaded, and every new container forks from it and shares pages copy-on-write. Software only, on installed servers.
why: Per-instance memory for interpreter, libraries and shared weights (often 200 MB-2 GB) is paid once per node, cutting container fleet DRAM 2-4x.

title: Model-on-ROM: frozen weights etched in 40 nm mask ROM
idea: Inverts 'weights must live in rewritable memory': a frozen foundation model's INT4 weights are etched as mask ROM on existing 40 nm logic lines (~0.01 um2 per bit, so a 7B model needs ~280 mm2 of bitcells across a few dies) next to small accelerators, leaving all DRAM for KV and activations.
why: Removes weight DRAM entirely for long-lived deployed models, using mature, plentiful capacity and no DRAM wafers.

title: Export idle host DRAM of GPU servers as far memory
idea: Inverts 'a server's DRAM serves only its own CPU': GPU servers carry 1-2 TB of host DRAM that sits mostly idle while the GPUs work from HBM. An RDMA far-memory daemon leases those idle bytes to neighboring CPU servers for swap and tiering over existing NICs.
why: Unlocks 30-60% of host DRAM in AI racks for the rest of the fleet with no new chips.

title: Recompute beats retain: drop KV between turns, then re-prefill
idea: Inverts 'prefill is expensive and KV is cheap': at 4x DRAM prices, holding a user's KV through human think time costs more per GB-hour than the prefill FLOPs to rebuild it. The server keeps only token text between turns, re-prefills on existing GPUs, and a cost model picks keep, spill or recompute per session.
why: Idle sessions are typically >90% of open sessions, so resident KV drops several-fold for chat fleets, in software only.

title: Weight radio: one DRAM read broadcast to 32 accelerators
idea: Inverts 'every accelerator needs its own copy of the weights': many small inference cards march in lockstep through the same layer while one shared DDR4 pool streams each weight tile once over a multicast fabric built from existing 28 nm FPGAs and SerDes. Each card applies the tile to its own batch.
why: Weight DRAM drops N-fold (e.g., 32x) across a pod, using trailing-node accelerators and legacy DRAM.

title: Learned indexes replace in-memory hash tables and B-trees
idea: Inverts 'an index stores keys and pointers': piecewise-linear models predict a key's position in a sorted array to within a small error window, replacing in-memory B-trees and hash indexes. Software only, on any existing CPU.
why: Index memory falls 10-100x for large key-value stores and databases, where indexes are often 20-40% of DRAM.

title: Reclaim ECC lanes for data and guard tensors with checksums
idea: Inverts 'every word needs hardware ECC': a 28 nm CXL controller uses the ECC chips' lanes as extra data capacity for regions holding ML weights and KV. Those regions are protected instead by per-tensor checksums, with a re-fetch from a golden copy on mismatch.
why: DDR5 RDIMMs spend 20% of their chips on ECC; reclaiming them for tolerant data adds ~25% usable capacity from modules already made.

title: Bytes-per-transaction disclosure standard for federal software procurement
idea: Inverts 'memory efficiency is a private engineering choice': a public benchmark and label, like Energy Star, reports peak and average DRAM per transaction for cloud services and enterprise software, and federal procurement favors top-quartile products.
why: Creates market pull for memory-lean software; cutting software footprint 20-30% equals years of new fab output, without a fab.

title: DIMM leasing: pull idle DRAM out of enterprise servers
idea: Inverts 'installed DRAM stays where it was first installed': a telemetry agent shows that enterprise servers use only ~40% of their installed memory. A broker buys or leases the surplus DIMMs, pulls them during maintenance windows and redeploys them to clouds and AI builders.
why: Hundreds of PB of DRAM sit underused in enterprise datacenters; recirculating 10-20% of it equals months of global output.

title: Router-predicted MoE expert paging from existing SSDs
idea: Inverts 'all experts must be resident': only hot experts stay in DRAM. A small predictor reads router logits from earlier layers and prefetches the likely next-layer experts from NVMe RAID on existing servers, hiding flash latency behind the current layer's compute.
why: MoE models activate 5-15% of experts per token, so DRAM holds ~20-30% of the weights instead of all of them: a 3-5x cut in weight memory.

title: Harvest LPDDR from recycled phones onto CXL cards
idea: Inverts 'consumer device memory dies with the device': e-waste recyclers desolder LPDDR4/4X packages from phones and laptops, reball and burn them in, and mount them on CXL cards with 28 nm controllers for slow capacity tiers.
why: Billions of retired devices hold 4-12 GB each, an exabyte-scale stranded bit supply that needs only existing OSAT lines and trailing-node controllers.

title: Wire-bonded 16-high stacks of trailing-node DRAM, no TSVs
idea: Inverts 'dense memory needs TSV stacking': staircase wire-bonded stacks of 16 thinned dies from mature DRAM nodes, built on existing OSAT lines, form capacity-only packages for CXL modules, where GB per slot matters more than bandwidth per package.
why: Avoids the HBM TSV area and yield tax and delivers high GB per module from existing fabs and packaging lines.

title: Per-application trained zstd dictionaries in kernel memory compression
idea: Inverts 'one generic compressor fits all memory': zswap/zram trains a zstd dictionary per workload class (Java heap, Python objects, protobufs) from sampled cold pages and recompresses cold pages with it on idle cores. Software on existing servers.
why: Dictionaries lift compression on small pages from ~2.5x to ~4x, freeing another 10-20% of DRAM fleet-wide.

title: Looped transformers reuse one block's weights many times
idea: Inverts 'each layer needs its own weights': models are retrained or distilled into a few shared blocks that execute repeatedly, with tiny per-iteration adapters, so depth costs FLOPs on existing GPUs instead of weight bytes.
why: Weight memory drops 4-12x for the same effective depth, freeing DRAM/HBM for KV and larger batches.

title: Texture-compression units repurposed to hold activations compressed
idea: Inverts 'GPU texture hardware is only for graphics': activations, KV blocks or embeddings are encoded into fixed-rate block-compressed texture formats (BC/ASTC-style) and read through the GPU's existing texture samplers, which decode them in hardware at full speed.
why: Fixed-rate 4-8x compression on tolerant tensors, using silicon already installed in billions of GPUs and no new chips.

title: Cold-byte reaper right-sizes heaps using idle-page tracking
idea: Inverts 'allocated means needed': page-idle tracking (DAMON or the idle bitmap) finds heap regions untouched for minutes, and an agent then lowers JVM -Xmx, Go GOMEMLIMIT and cache sizes per service, rolling back on latency regressions. Software only.
why: Fleet audits typically find 20-40% of resident memory cold; right-sizing frees that DRAM in servers already installed.

title: Expiry-dated memory: allocations carry leases that must be renewed
idea: Inverts 'an allocation lives until someone frees it': the allocator gives every long-lived block a lease renewed by access. Unrenewed blocks are compressed first, then paged out to flash and reported as suspected leaks with their allocation stack. Software only, on installed servers.
why: Long-running services leak or bloat 10-30% over their uptime; leases cap that growth with no hardware.
